implementation_notes: Swift Concurrency's `actor` absorbs most of what the classic structure provides, and the schema's 'idiomatic' rating means exactly that: a simpler local mechanism replaces the full form. An actor serialises access to its mutable state, so composite updates inside an actor method are atomic with respect to other actors without a lock, without a read set, and without automatic re-execution - because suspension points are explicit and rare, which is also why actors do not starve the way STM transactions can. Two Swift specifics sharpen this. First, actor reentrancy: `await` inside an actor method releases the actor at the suspension point, so a long-running method can be interleaved; the Swift analogue of STM's discipline is to keep `await` out of the critical section or to re-validate state after every `await`. Second, where genuine lock-free publish is wanted - the validate-then-act shape STM uses for commit - `ManagedAtomic` from swift-atomics gives `compareExchange(expected:desired:)` returning the previous value, which is the exact primitive; pair it with a class holding an immutable value so 'changed' is pointer identity. The classic STM structure is still justified when several threads must mutate one object without ownership passing to any of them.
pitfalls: Awaiting inside an actor method and assuming the actor is still held afterwards - reentrancy means it is not, and state read before the await may be stale after it.
Reaching for ManagedAtomic when an actor would be simpler: atomics give you atomicity without ownership, which is exactly what makes composite invariants hard.
Comparing a pointer with === to detect a change and assuming that implies the contents are unchanged; a value type mutated in place behind an UnsafeMutablePointer defeats it.
Using @unchecked Sendable on a mutable class to silence the compiler, which reintroduces the data race the actor was avoiding.
Retrying a transaction without a fairness mechanism, so one caller can starve; actors serialise in arrival order, which is a different and often better guarantee.
